questions.q: In an API call, what's the difference between the client and the server?
options: There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
The client only runs on mobile phones
The client sends the request; the server processes it and sends back the response
The server always asks the questions
questions.explain: The client is the program asking the question; the server is the program that does the work and answers it.

questions.q: In the Swagger UI documentation screenshot, what does the color coding on each endpoint (green, orange, blue) represent?
options: How popular each endpoint is
The HTTP method — e.g. green for POST, orange for PUT, blue for GET
Whether the endpoint requires payment
The response time of each endpoint
questions.explain: Swagger UI color-codes each endpoint row by its HTTP method, a convention that shows up across many documentation tools.

questions.q: Why is POST /orders considered NOT idempotent, while DELETE /orders/1001 IS idempotent?
options: POST always fails on the second call, while DELETE always succeeds
Calling POST /orders twice creates two separate orders, while calling DELETE /orders/1001 twice ends with the same result (the order gone)
POST and DELETE are actually both idempotent
Idempotency only applies to GET requests
questions.explain: Each POST call creates a brand-new resource (a different end state each time), while repeated DELETE calls on the same resource all end with it gone.

questions.q: What does REST stand for, and what kind of thing is it?
options: Representational State Transfer — an architectural style for designing APIs, not a protocol or piece of software
Remote Execution Service Toolkit, a programming language
A file format for storing structured data
A protocol that requires a persistent connection between client and server
questions.explain: REST is Roy Fielding's architectural style — a set of conventions for API design — not a protocol, product, or format.

questions.q: Why does {"name": "Ada", "role": "admin",} fail to parse as JSON?
options: Because "role" is not a valid key name
Because of the trailing comma after the last item, which JSON does not allow
Because JSON doesn't support string values
It actually parses fine
questions.explain: JSON strictly forbids a trailing comma after the final key/value pair or array item — one of the most common hand-written JSON errors.

questions.q: What are the six data types JSON supports?
options: String, number, boolean, null, object, array
String, integer, float, date, object, array
Text, number, true, false, comment, function
String, number, boolean, undefined, object, array
questions.explain: JSON's entire type system is exactly six types: string, number, boolean, null, object, and array — nothing else, including no native date or function type.

questions.q: What is JSON Schema used for?
options: Compressing JSON files to save bandwidth
Describing what a piece of JSON is allowed to look like — required fields, types, and valid values
Converting JSON into XML
Encrypting JSON request bodies
questions.explain: JSON Schema is a specification for describing the shape and constraints a piece of JSON must satisfy — itself written in JSON.

questions.q: Given {"orders": [{"id": 1001}, {"id": 1002}]}, what does orders[1].id evaluate to?
options: The entire orders array
An error, since arrays can't contain objects
questions.explain: orders[1] steps into the array at position 1 (the second item, zero-indexed), and .id reads that object's id field: 1002.

questions.q: What transport does Anthropic's streaming Messages API use?
options: Server-Sent Events (SSE) over a kept-open HTTP connection
WebSockets
A new TCP connection per word
FTP
questions.explain: Streaming uses SSE: plain HTTP kept open, with event:/data: pairs pushed down the same connection. (Not WebSockets.)

questions.q: Why does pagination exist at all?
options: Because JSON cannot represent more than 100 items
To improve response compression
So a server never has to send (and a client never has to process) an unbounded result set in one response
It's required by the HTTP specification
questions.explain: Pagination splits large result sets into manageable pages fetched one request at a time, rather than one enormous response.

questions.q: What does the Anthropic Messages API's usage.input_tokens field tell you?
options: How many tokens your prompt/messages consumed, which affects your bill
How many words were in the model's reply
The maximum tokens the model is allowed to generate
The model's version number
questions.explain: usage.input_tokens counts tokens consumed by what you sent in; usage.output_tokens counts what the model generated back.

questions.q: What syntax does a tool's input_schema use to describe its arguments?
options: Real JSON Schema (type, properties, required)
A proprietary Anthropic-only syntax unrelated to JSON Schema
Plain English only
XML
questions.explain: input_schema reuses standard JSON Schema — the same type/properties/required structure covered in Chapter 2.

It permanently changes the AIClient class definition
It replaces session.post with a stand-in that returns the fake response instead of making a real call
It deletes the session object
questions.explain: unittest.mock's patch.object swaps out session.post for a mock during the test, so no real network call happens.

questions.q: What is 'proactive throttling', as described in this lesson?
options: Waiting for a 429 error before taking any action
Disabling retries entirely
Slowing down your own request rate before you actually hit the limit, by watching -remaining headers
Always waiting exactly 60 seconds between every request
questions.explain: Proactive throttling means easing off based on the -remaining headers before a 429 ever happens, rather than only reacting after the fact.

questions.q: What happens in the example loop when a non-retryable error (like a 400) comes back?
options: resp.raise_for_status() raises immediately — no retry happens
It's silently ignored and None is returned
It retries exactly like a 429 would
The program exits without an exception
questions.explain: Only 429/5xx trigger the retry branch; anything else falls through to raise_for_status(), which raises right away.

questions.q: What advantage does requests.Session() have over calling requests.post() directly each time?
options: It reuses the underlying connection and headers across multiple calls
It automatically retries failed requests forever
It removes the need for an API key
It converts JSON responses into XML
questions.explain: A Session reuses the connection (and configured headers) rather than rebuilding everything from scratch on every single call.

questions.q: According to this lesson, are streaming and tool calling required for the capstone to count as done?
options: Yes, both are strict requirements
No — they're strong additions / stretch goals, not strict requirements
Only tool calling is required, not streaming
Neither topic is relevant to this capstone at all
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly separates the five required items from streaming and tool calling, which are called out as strong additions rather than requirements.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what three things should a one-minute interview answer about the capstone include?
options: The total line count, the programming language, and the file names
Only a list of every method name
The exact salary you expect to earn from this skill
What it does, the hardest decision made, and how you proved it works
questions.explain: The lesson recommends a concise structure: what the project does, the hardest design decision, and the evidence (tests) that it works.
